variables.PATH_WIDTH: Medium uniform weight (around three to four points, roughly six pixels at a thousand-pixel longest edge)

prompt.task: Create a clean, premium-quality, print-ready step-by-step drawing worksheet that teaches a child in {{TARGET_AGE_RANGE}} how to draw a {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} in exactly {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} progressive stages. The final image must look like a polished page from a children's how-to-draw activity book that a real child can follow with a pencil — every stage must be physically drawable on top of the previous one without ever erasing.
hard_constraints: Render exactly {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} progressive drawing stages — never fewer, never more.

Scale lock: every stage depicts the same character at the same size. The silhouette bounding box is identical in every stage. A stage with fewer lines must never appear smaller than a stage with more lines.
Identity lock: every stage depicts the same species, same breed, same pose, same accessories, same silhouette. No species drift. No accessory or distinguishing mark appearing mid-sequence.
Stroke rules: every stroke is pure {{STROKE_COLOR}}, exactly {{PATH_WIDTH}}, uniform from start to end. No tapering, no pressure variation, no thinner detail lines, no thicker outer outlines.

Strict accumulation: each stage is treated as a pixel-identical copy of the previous stage with only freshly added lines on top. Never redraw, resize, rotate, translate, mirror, smooth, simplify, sharpen, clean up, refine, restyle, replace, or reinterpret any line that already appeared in an earlier stage. If you need a previously drawn line in a later stage, you reuse the exact same line — same coordinates, same length, same curvature, same endpoints, same thickness — not a new version of it.

Orientation lock: the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} faces the same direction in every single stage of the worksheet. The character is never flipped horizontally (left-right mirrored) and never flipped vertically (upside-down mirrored) between stages. If the character faces left in stage one, it faces left in every following stage. If it faces right in stage one, it faces right in every following stage. Same head tilt, same body angle, same eye direction, same nose direction, same tail direction, same paw or limb orientation in every stage.

No-erase rule: a child following these stages with a pencil must never have to erase or modify any line they already drew. Every later stage must add new lines that fit cleanly around or attach to existing lines without crossing through, replacing, or contradicting them.
Background is fully {{BACKGROUND}} across the entire canvas, pure and uniform, with no transparency, no off-white, no cream, and no paper texture.
No text, letters, digits, captions, labels, titles, logos, or watermarks anywhere on the canvas.

Face-on-final-stage rule: if the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} has a face (animals, humans, dolls, toys with faces, fruits or vehicles drawn with kawaii faces, robots, monsters, mythical creatures, anything cartoon-style with eyes), then ALL facial features — eyes, eyebrows, pupils, irises, eye highlights, eyelashes, nose, nostrils, snout details, muzzle line, mouth, lips, smile line, tongue, teeth, fangs, beak details, whiskers, freckles, blush spots, cheek dots, chin line — must appear ONLY in the FINAL stage and in NO earlier stage. The earlier stages may show the head shape, ears, hair, mane, horns, antlers, body, limbs, tail, accessories, and other non-facial identity markers, but the face itself must remain completely blank until the final stage. If the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} has no face (a plain bottle, a plain cup, a plain ball, a plain backpack with no kawaii face, a plain piece of furniture), this rule does not apply and finishing details fill the final stage as usual.
stage_to_stage_visual_continuity_critica: READ THIS BEFORE DRAWING ANY STAGE. The single most important rule of this worksheet is visual continuity from one stage to the next. A child must be able to look at any stage and see THE EXACT SAME DRAWING they saw in the previous stage, with new lines added on top — nothing else changed.

Mental model: imagine that stage one was drawn on a real sheet of paper. To produce stage two, that exact sheet of paper is photocopied 1:1 onto a fresh sheet, and only then are the new stage-two lines added on top of the photocopy. To produce stage three, the stage-two sheet is photocopied 1:1 again, and only the new stage-three lines are added. And so on. Every stage is the photocopy of the previous stage plus only the new strokes of that stage. There is no other source of difference between stages.

Every line introduced in any earlier stage must remain in every following stage with all of these properties IDENTICAL: position on the canvas, length, width, height, orientation, rotation, curvature, smoothness, every bump and every dip, every endpoint, every junction with another line, line thickness, and line color. Not approximately the same — exactly the same.

Do not improve, polish, neaten, smooth, round, sharpen, simplify, regularize, symmetrize, beautify, redraw more carefully, or visually upgrade any earlier line in a later stage. Even if the earlier line looks slightly imperfect or could be drawn better, it must be reproduced unchanged. The earlier stage is the source of truth — never the target of revision.

Do not nudge, shift, slide, drift, recenter, rebalance, re-anchor, or reposition any earlier line by even a single pixel. The character's anchor point in stage two is exactly the anchor point of stage one. The character's anchor point in stage three is exactly the anchor point of stage two. And so on.

Do not rescale any earlier line. The head circle from stage one is the same circle in stage two — same diameter, same center, same shape, same outline thickness. Not slightly larger, not slightly smaller, not slightly rounder, not slightly more oval.

Do not flip, mirror, or change the facing direction of the character or any of its parts between stages. The whole character keeps the exact same orientation in every stage — never horizontally mirrored (left to right or right to left), never vertically mirrored (upside down or right side up swap), never rotated by any angle. Every individual line keeps the exact same direction it had when first drawn: a curve that opens to the left in stage one still opens to the left in every later stage; a tail that sweeps to the right in an early stage still sweeps to the right in every later stage; a face looking left in an early stage still looks left in every later stage. Mirroring the character as a whole, or mirroring any part of it, is treated as a complete failure of the worksheet.

Do not restyle any earlier line. If stage one's head outline has a particular wobble or a particular curve, stage two's head outline has that exact same wobble and that exact same curve. Do not switch from a hand-drawn feel to a vector feel between stages, or from a slightly loose curve to a perfect arc, or from one line weight to another.

When a later stage adds a feature that touches or attaches to an earlier line, the new feature must connect to the earlier line at the exact endpoints already present in that line, with the earlier line itself remaining 100% unchanged. Do not extend, shorten, or re-end any earlier line to make the connection cleaner — instead, plan the earlier line so the connection is already clean (see the welcoming-socket section below).

If at any point you find yourself wanting to redraw an earlier line because the new feature would fit better, STOP. The correct fix is never to redraw the earlier line — the correct fix is to go back and re-plan the earlier stage so the line was placed correctly from the start.

Stage validation test: if you mentally subtract a later stage from the previous stage, the only difference must be the freshly added lines of the later stage. Subtracting must NEVER reveal that an earlier line moved, resized, rotated, smoothed, or changed style. If subtraction reveals any change to an earlier line, the worksheet is wrong and must be redone.

Forbidden continuity failures: head circle slightly larger or smaller in a later stage; body oval slightly more rounded or more elongated in a later stage; an earlier wobbly outline replaced with a smoother one in a later stage; a feature in a later stage drawn over the earlier line as a corrected version; the character drifting a few pixels left, right, up, or down between stages; the character's center of gravity shifting between stages; the line weight of an earlier line getting thicker or thinner in a later stage; an earlier line being broken into segments or fused into one continuous curve in a later stage.
step_to_step_completion_ease: When planning each stage, think about how the NEXT stage will be added by a child holding a pencil. The child should look at the current stage, immediately see where the new lines belong, and be able to add them naturally — without confusion, without erasing, and without having to interpret an unusual or broken-looking base shape.

What actually makes a stage easy to continue is good PROPORTION and good POSITION of the base shapes — not literal pre-cut gaps in the outline. A head drawn at the right size and position already implies where ears, mane, hair, eyes, or a muzzle will go. A body drawn at the right length and angle already implies where legs and tail will go. The child reads these implied attachment zones automatically.

Default to clean, simple, friendly closed silhouettes in every early stage. A clean closed oval head is correct, even when ears, mane, or hair will be added later — children naturally draw ears that sit on top of a head and hair that flows along a head curve. They do NOT need a pre-cut notch to know where to put a new feature.

Do NOT damage the base silhouette with awkward notches, sudden cuts, slits, scoops, or unexplained gaps just because a future feature will attach there. A broken-looking base shape confuses the child far more than a clean closed shape ever does. A child seeing a strange slit in stage one will not understand why it is there and will not know what to do with it.

Two completion patterns are equally valid; choose whichever produces the cleanest, most child-friendly worksheet for the subject: (1) the new feature in the later stage attaches OUTSIDE the earlier closed shape, touching its outline cleanly along the surface (ears sitting on top of a closed head, legs dropping from a closed body, a tail curling away from a closed body, hair lying along the top of a closed head, a mane flowing down the side of a closed neck); (2) the new feature in the later stage sits ENTIRELY INSIDE the earlier closed shape (eyes, nose, mouth, cheeks, spots, simple inner markings, fur swirls). Both are good. Closed clean silhouettes are the safe default.

Only use a genuinely open shape (for example a cup drawn as an open U so icing fills the top, or an envelope drawn open so a card slides out) when the open shape itself is a recognizable, intentional, friendly choice — not a closed shape with a piece chopped out. If in doubt, draw the clean closed base shape.

If a later stage adds a feature that touches an earlier outline (ears, hair, limbs, tail, mane), the new feature simply touches that outline at its surface. The earlier outline stays exactly as it was, and the new feature is drawn alongside it without crossing it inward. This is the natural way children draw — touching at the edge, not piercing through.

Self-test before finalizing any stage: would a 5-to-8 year old looking only at this stage understand it as a clean recognizable shape? Would they be able to add the next features by simply touching or filling, without erasing and without wondering why a notch is there? If the answer is yes, the stage is well-planned. If the stage looks broken, scooped, slit, or arbitrarily interrupted, redo it as a clean closed shape.
canvas_and_output: Output resolution: render the image at exactly {{RESOLUTION_QUALITY}} — do not upscale, do not super-sample, do not produce any resolution higher than {{RESOLUTION_QUALITY}}. The final pixel dimensions of the output image must correspond to {{RESOLUTION_QUALITY}}, with crisp sharp linework calibrated for activity-book printing at that resolution.

The canvas is a single open page — no visible panels, no visible frames, no visible boxes, no visible borders, no visible grid lines, no visible dividers of any kind between the stages or around the outer edge.
layout: Place the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} stages in a staggered N-shaped reading flow across the canvas, following the sequence of stages from first to last.

For a four-stage worksheet, use this exact arrangement: the first stage sits in the upper-left area of the canvas; the second stage sits in the lower-left area, below the first stage but shifted slightly to the right so that its center does not sit directly under the first stage; the third stage sits in the upper-right area; the fourth stage sits in the lower-right area, below the third stage but shifted slightly further to the right so that its center does not sit directly under the third stage.
The reading flow goes: first stage → second stage → third stage → fourth stage, tracing a staggered N shape across the canvas.

For a stage count other than four, keep the same staggered N logic — alternating upper and lower positions while progressively drifting from left to right — and distribute the stages evenly across the canvas.

Keep airy, generous spacing between stages with comfortable outer margins around the whole composition. Stages may visually approach each other at their outer edges but the drawn content of one stage must never overlap the drawn content of another stage.

The {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} is anchored at the same relative position and the same scale within every stage area. No shifting, drifting, floating, or recentering of the character between stages — every stage reads as a transparent overlay of the next, same anchor, same scale, only new lines added on top.
arrows_critical: Arrows are CRITICAL. Get the count, the color, the style, and the direction exactly right. Do not improvise.

Total arrow count: draw EXACTLY {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} minus 1 arrows on the entire canvas — never more, never fewer. For a four-stage worksheet this means EXACTLY 3 arrows. For a three-stage worksheet, EXACTLY 2 arrows. For a five-stage worksheet, EXACTLY 4 arrows. Count them before finalizing.

Each arrow connects exactly one consecutive pair of stages: arrow 1 goes from stage 1 to stage 2, arrow 2 goes from stage 2 to stage 3, arrow 3 goes from stage 3 to stage 4, and so on. Never draw an arrow between non-consecutive stages. Never draw an arrow from the final stage back to any earlier stage. Never draw a closing or looping arrow that returns to stage 1.

Arrow style: dotted line (a sequence of small round dots evenly spaced), softly curved (a gentle arc, not a sharp angle, not a perfectly straight segment), with a single small simple arrowhead at the destination end only. No double-headed arrows. No solid lines. No dashed lines. No thick painted strokes. No fancy decorative arrows.
Arrow color: every arrow and every arrowhead is exactly {{ARROW_COLOR}} — a soft medium gray. Never black. Never any other color.

Arrow size: arrows are clearly visible but visually quieter than the character linework. The dot diameter and arrowhead size are noticeably smaller than {{PATH_WIDTH}} so the eye reads the character as the main subject and the arrows as secondary guidance.

Arrow placement: each arrow sits in the empty space between the two stages it connects, following the staggered N reading flow. Arrows never cross any drawn character line, never cross another arrow, and never overlap the silhouette of any stage.

Forbidden arrow mistakes: drawing four or more arrows in a four-stage worksheet; drawing a closing arrow from the final stage; drawing any arrow that loops back; drawing duplicate arrows between the same pair of stages; drawing arrows in pure black; drawing solid or dashed arrows instead of dotted; drawing straight arrows instead of softly curved; drawing arrows with arrowheads at both ends; drawing arrows that cross the character or another arrow.
step_construction_logic: Before drawing any stage, decide whether the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} has a face. A subject HAS a face if it is an animal, a human, a doll, a toy with eyes, a kawaii-style fruit or vegetable drawn with eyes, a kawaii-style vehicle or object drawn with eyes, a robot with a face, a monster, or a mythical creature. A subject DOES NOT have a face if it is a plain inanimate object drawn realistically with no kawaii eyes (a plain bottle, a plain cup, a plain ball, a plain backpack, a plain piece of furniture, a plain musical instrument with no eyes, a plain plant or tree). This decision controls the role of the third and fourth stages described below.

First stage shows only the primary simplified volume — the main head mass, body mass, or largest base shape. No facial features, no accessories, no small details. The first-stage shape is drawn as a clean, friendly, closed silhouette with proportions and positioning that already imply where future features will naturally attach.

Middle stages before the third stage extend the base with large and medium structural shapes only, with no facial features yet. New external shapes (ears, mane, hair, limbs, tail) attach naturally along the outside of the previous stage's silhouette by touching it at the surface — the previous outline is never broken, notched, or interrupted to make room for them.

Third stage rule for face-bearing subjects: when the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} has a face, the third stage adds NON-FACIAL identity markers and structural details that make the species or character recognizable WITHOUT yet drawing any part of the face. These can include: hair locks or fringe, mane segments, fur tufts or fur direction lines, spots or stripes pattern, scales pattern, feather rows, horn or antler details, ear inner shapes, paw pads, claws, hooves, fingers, accessory details (collars, bows, hats, glasses frames WITHOUT lenses-as-eyes), clothing folds, wing feathers, fin rays, shell segments, tail tufts, decorative markings on the body. The HEAD area in stage three contains only non-facial elements (such as hair, hat, ears, horns, tuft on top of the head) and the face area itself remains completely BLANK — no eyes, no nose, no mouth, no eyebrows, no whiskers, no cheeks, no muzzle line, no chin line, no smile, nothing on the face surface.

Third stage rule for face-less subjects: when the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} does not have a face, the third stage adds the medium structural details and identity markers appropriate to the object (handle of a cup, label area of a bottle, laces of a shoe, buttons of a shirt, panel lines of a vehicle without eyes, branches of a tree, etc.) — exactly as it would in a normal worksheet.

Fourth stage rule for face-bearing subjects: when the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} has a face, the fourth stage adds ALL facial features for the first time — eyes (with pupils and any highlights), eyebrows if present, nose or snout details, mouth or smile line, tongue or teeth if shown, whiskers, blush or cheek dots, freckles, beak details, fangs, chin line — together with any remaining small finishing details elsewhere on the body. The face appearing in stage four is the moment the character finally comes alive: a child finishing this stage instantly recognizes the personality of the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} for the first time. All facial features sit entirely inside the head shape; the head outline is never modified to accommodate them.

Fourth stage rule for face-less subjects: when the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} does not have a face, the fourth stage completes the character with the small finishing details that were not yet present (small surface details, texture hints expressed as discrete lines, small accessory details, etc.).

Every stage must clearly build toward the final complete {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} as a pixel-identical photocopy of the previous stage with only new lines added on top — no line from any earlier stage may be altered, redrawn, repositioned, rescaled, restyled, smoothed, or upgraded in any way, and the child must never be forced to erase anything they previously drew.
progression_balance: The visual change from one stage to the next must be immediately obvious to a child at a glance — never subtle, never minor.
The amount of new content added at each stage must be roughly equal across the entire sequence.
Do not concentrate the majority of the drawing into one or two stages while leaving other stages nearly unchanged.
Do not apply a large change in one stage followed by only a tiny finishing touch in the next.
Every stage transition must feel equally significant and equally rewarding for the child.

Special note for face-bearing subjects: even though the face is reserved for the final stage, the third stage must still carry a substantial amount of new content (hair, mane, fur, spots, accessories, paws, claws, ear inner shapes, tail details, etc.) so it does not feel emptier than the other stages. The third stage is the non-facial identity stage, not a low-content waiting stage.
style_and_lines: Drawing style: {{DRAWING_STYLE}}, interpreted in a simplified workbook-friendly way rather than a highly detailed commercial illustration.
Clean two-dimensional cartoon line art, coloring-book-style outlines, smooth, readable, and print-friendly.
Cute, rounded, child-safe shapes appropriate for {{TARGET_AGE_RANGE}} unless {{DRAWING_STYLE}} naturally requires a slightly different but still kid-appropriate simplification.
Clear silhouette, simple construction, beginner-friendly, easy to imitate with a pencil or crayon.
No shading, no color fill, no gradients, no gray tones (other than the {{ARROW_COLOR}} arrows), no shadows, no textures, no sketch effect, and no painterly rendering.
character_design: The {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} must look cute, simple, friendly, and appealing to children in {{TARGET_AGE_RANGE}}.
Simplified proportions, open readable shapes, minimal overlaps, and no confusing construction.
Avoid realism, complex anatomy, and excessive detail.
The final character must feel playful, approachable, educational, and confidence-building for kids.
final_checklist: Before finalizing the output, confirm each of the following. If any check fails, redo the worksheet.
Confirm that exactly {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} stages are visible on the canvas.
Confirm that the character in the first stage and the final stage occupy the same silhouette bounding-box area at the same scale.
Confirm that every character line is pure {{STROKE_COLOR}} and exactly {{PATH_WIDTH}}, uniform throughout the worksheet.

Confirm that each stage equals a pixel-identical photocopy of the previous stage plus only newly added lines — nothing moved, nothing resized, nothing rotated, nothing mirrored, nothing smoothed, nothing simplified, nothing redrawn, nothing retraced, nothing restyled, nothing polished, nothing upgraded, nothing nudged.

Mentally subtract each later stage from its previous stage. Confirm that the only visible difference is the freshly added lines of that stage, with every earlier line still in exactly the same position, size, orientation, curvature, and thickness as before. If subtraction reveals any other change to an earlier line, redo the worksheet.
Confirm that the character's anchor position and overall scale are pixel-identical between every consecutive pair of stages, with no drift in any direction.

Confirm the orientation lock: the character faces the exact same direction in every stage, has not been horizontally mirrored, has not been vertically mirrored, and has not been rotated between any two stages. Every individual line keeps the exact same direction it had when first drawn (curves opening the same way, tail sweeping the same way, face looking the same way). If any stage shows the character or any of its parts mirrored or rotated relative to an earlier stage, redo the worksheet.

Confirm the no-erase rule: every new line in every later stage either touches an earlier outline cleanly along its surface from outside, or sits entirely inside an existing closed shape — without crossing, breaking, or replacing any earlier line.

Confirm that every base shape in every early stage is a clean, friendly, recognizable closed silhouette — not damaged by awkward notches, slits, scoops, or arbitrary gaps. If a stage looks broken or interrupted in any way, redo it as a clean closed shape.
Confirm that species, pose, silhouette, and accessories match across every stage with no drift.

Face-on-final-stage check: if the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} has a face, confirm that NO facial feature (no eyes, no pupils, no eyebrows, no eyelashes, no nose, no nostrils, no muzzle line, no mouth, no smile line, no lips, no tongue, no teeth, no fangs, no whiskers, no blush, no cheek dots, no chin line, no beak details) appears in stage one, stage two, OR stage three of a four-stage worksheet. The face must be entirely BLANK in stage three. ALL facial features must appear for the first time only in the FINAL stage. If any facial feature is visible in stage three or earlier, redo the worksheet.

Face-less-subject check: if the {{DRAWING_SUBJECT}} does not have a face (a plain object with no kawaii eyes), confirm that the four stages still distribute new content evenly without any single stage being nearly empty.

Confirm that the layout follows the staggered N path, with the second stage shifted slightly to the right below the first stage, and the fourth stage shifted slightly to the right below the third stage.
Count the arrows on the canvas. Confirm that the total number of arrows equals exactly {{DRAWING_STEPS_NUMBER}} minus 1. For a four-stage worksheet this number must be exactly 3.
Confirm that every arrow is dotted (small round dots evenly spaced), softly curved, with a single arrowhead at the destination end only, and is colored exactly {{ARROW_COLOR}}.
Confirm that no arrow connects non-consecutive stages, no arrow loops back from the final stage, and no two arrows connect the same pair of stages.
Confirm that the background is fully {{BACKGROUND}} and that no text, numerals, labels, frames, borders, boxes, grid lines, or dividers appear anywhere on the canvas.
